title: Nuclear receptor Nr1d1 links sleep deprivation to intestinal homeostasis via microbiota-derived taurine

sections.abstract:
Sleep deficiency significantly compromises human health, with the gut being particularly susceptible. However, the molecular mechanisms by which gut microbiota mediate sleep deprivation-induced intestinal dysfunction remain largely undefined. In this study, we employed a chronic sleep deprivation (CSD) mouse model to investigate the impact of sleep loss on intestinal integrity and microbial composition.

The CSD mouse model was established using the modified multiple platform (rotating rod) method. Colon histomorphology was assessed by hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining. Expression levels of barrier proteins (Occludin, Claudin-1) and circadian regulators (Nr1d1, Bmal1) were evaluated via Western blot or immunohistochemistry (IHC). Gut microbiota composition and stability were analyzed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and the causal role of microbiota in CSD-induced barrier damage was assessed through fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of intestinal epithelial tissues identified differentially expressed genes and enriched pathways. Untargeted metabolomics was employed to investigate key differential metabolites (Taurine). Additionally, taurine was supplemented in vivo to explore its efficacy and mechanism in alleviating intestinal barrier damage in CSD mice.

CSD led to pronounced colon shortening and significant downregulation of the epithelial barrier proteins Occludin and Claudin-1, indicative of impaired intestinal barrier function. Moreover, CSD exacerbated symptoms of chemically induced colitis and induced gut microbiota dysbiosis. Mechanistically, FMT from CSD mice into antibiotic-treated recipients recapitulated intestinal inflammation, confirming the pathogenic role of the altered microbiota. Transcriptomic analysis revealed significant enrichment of genes involved in circadian rhythm pathways, notably a marked suppression of the circadian nuclear receptor Nr1d1, a key regulator of intestinal homeostasis. Complementary untargeted metabolomic profiling identified taurine as a microbiota-derived metabolite significantly reduced by CSD. In vivo taurine supplementation restored Nr1d1 expression, reinforced epithelial barrier integrity, and decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine production.

Together, these findings reveal a gut microbiota–taurine–Nr1d1 axis underlying sleep deprivation-induced intestinal barrier dysfunction, and suggest that therapeutic modulation of taurine levels or circadian pathways may offer novel strategies to prevent or treat sleep-related gastrointestinal disorders.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12967-025-07089-8.

Keywords: Sleep deprivation, Nuclear receptor, Gut microbiota, Taurine, Circadian rhythm
sections.introduction:
Sleep is an essential physiological process that maintains systemic homeostasis. Inadequate sleep quality compromises the body’s defense mechanisms, increasing vulnerability to various diseases. Currently, more than 30% of adults report sleeping fewer than six hours per night, with sleep deprivation commonly manifests as insomnia, behaviorally induced insufficient sleep syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea syndrome [ 1 , 2 ]. Accumulating evidence demonstrates that chronic sleep deprivation exerts widespread deleterious effects on health, including cognitive impairment, endocrine dysregulation, disruption of circadian rhythms, and immune dysfunction [ 3 – 6 ]. Among these adverse outcomes, the impact of sleep deprivation on gut health has received growing attention. Recent studies indicate that insufficient sleep exacerbates the progression of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and impedes its remission [ 7 , 8 ]. Clinically, individuals with IBD often exhibit impaired sleep quality, suggesting a bidirectional and tightly linked relationship between sleep and gut health [ 7 ]. Nevertheless, despite increasing recognition of this interaction, the molecular mechanisms by which sleep deficiency contributes to intestinal pathology remain poorly understood and warrant further investigation.

Alterations in the gut microbiota represent a pivotal mechanism linking sleep deprivation to impaired intestinal health. Individuals who frequently stay up late exhibit significant alterations in gut microbial composition, characterized by a reduction in beneficial bacteria and an increase in pathogenic species [ 9 , 10 ]. This dysbiosis disrupts intestinal homeostasis primarily through its impact on the intestinal epithelium. Sleep deprivation-induced microbial imbalance compromises mucosal barrier function and increases intestinal susceptibility to damage [ 11 , 12 ]. These observations underscore the critical role of gut microbiota and its metabolites in mediating the detrimental effects of sleep deprivation on intestinal health. Given the high prevalence of insufficient sleep and its profound impact on gastrointestinal disorders, investigating how the gut microbiota and its metabolites contribute to sleep deprivation-induced intestinal dysfunction is necessary. Among these, taurine—closely linked to gut microbiota metabolism. As a sulfur-containing, conditionally essential amino acid, it conjugates with bile acids to form tauroconjugated bile acids, which are critical for the emulsification, digestion, and absorption of lipids and fat-soluble vitamins in the small intestine [ 13 , 14 ]. However, research on the involvement of taurine in chronic sleep deprivation-induced intestinal barrier dysfunction remains relatively scarce, warranting in-depth investigation.

Nuclear receptors constitute a class of soluble proteins predominantly localized in the cytoplasm or nucleus that modulate gene transcription by binding to specific DNA sequences known as hormone response elements, thereby either activating or repressing target gene expression [ 15 , 16 ]. As key transcriptional regulators, nuclear receptors play essential roles in maintaining intestinal health and regulating gut microbiota composition and function [ 17 ]. For instance, the nuclear receptors PPARγ and FXR influence gut microbial communities by modulating intestinal epithelial barrier integrity, inflammatory responses, and metabolic pathways [ 18 , 19 ]. Importantly, nuclear receptors serve as critical molecular hubs that mediate the crosstalk between host-derived or microbial metabolites and intestinal health.

The circadian clock is a fundamental biological system that regulates daily physiological rhythms through a network of core clock genes and their protein products. Among these, NR1D1 (also known as REV-ERBα) is a nuclear receptor that serves as a critical component of the circadian machinery and metabolic regulation. We previously demonstrated that loss of NR1D1 exacerbates dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, underscoring its essential role in maintaining intestinal homeostasis and circadian rhythm integrity [ 20 ]. NR1D1 preserves gut immune balance by negatively regulating NF-κB signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome [ 21 ]. Systemic knockout of Nr1d1 in mice leads to increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IL-1β , accompanied by microglial depletion and immune dysfunction [ 22 ]. These findings collectively highlight the pivotal role of NR1D1 in coordinating circadian rhythm, immune, and microbial networks that safeguard intestinal health.

In this study, we aim to determine how sleep deprivation disrupts intestinal barrier function and exacerbates colitis in mice. We investigate whether gut microbiota alterations under sleep-deprived conditions mediate this effect, focusing on microbiota-derived taurine as a candidate metabolite. Furthermore, we will evaluate whether taurine influences intestinal homeostasis via the nuclear receptor NR1D1. These investigations may provide a mechanistic link between circadian disruption, microbial metabolism, and intestinal inflammation.
sections.methods:
Male C57BL/6 J mice (8 weeks old, 22 ± 2 g body weight) were obtained from the Guangdong Provincial Medical Laboratory Animal Center. The animals were maintained in a controlled environment with a constant temperature of 22 ± 2 °C and a 12-h light/dark cycle, with free access to standard rodent chow and water. All mice were acclimatized to the housing conditions for at least one week prior to the commencement of experimental procedures. In compliance with the 3Rs principles (Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement), every effort was made to minimize animal suffering and to optimize the number of animals used, while ensuring the robustness and reproducibility of the experimental outcomes. The animal experiments in this study were supported by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and Jennio Biotech Co., Ltd. The approval number was #JENNIO-IACUC-2025-A022.

To induce a chronic sleep deprivation (CSD) model, mice were housed individually in polycarbonate cylindrical cages fitted with motorized rotating rods (mechanical intervention) (XR-XS108, Xinruan Information Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) [ 23 , 24 ]. Prior to the initiation of the experiment, all animals were acclimatized to the apparatus for a minimum of 24 h under standard conditions, including access to fresh bedding, food, and water ad libitum. Sleep deprivation was achieved by continuous rotation of the rods at a speed of approximately 8 rpm, with the direction of rotation randomized at regular intervals to prevent habituation and to disrupt sustained sleep. The CSD protocol was implemented daily from 18:00 (ZT10) to 14:00 the following day (ZT6), resulting in 20 h of sleep deprivation per day. During the remaining 4 h period (14:00 to 18:00), the rotation was halted to allow for a brief rest interval. This regimen was consistently applied over a period of 21 consecutive days to establish the CSD model, and experiments consist of 6 mice per group.

To construct a mouse model of colitis, we administered 2.5% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) to the mice for a duration of one week, with 6 mice per group. Specifically, DSS (A6743241, iV, Shanghai, China) was dissolved in distilled water at a concentration of 2.5%, which served as the drinking water for the mice. This solution was replaced with fresh DSS daily. In the chronic sleep deprivation combined with DSS group (DSS + CSD), mice were subjected to sleep deprivation while consuming the 2.5% DSS, whereas the control group received pure water. Body weight was measured daily at the same time, and observations were made regarding rectal bleeding and stool characteristics. The symptoms of colitis were quantified using the Disease Activity Index (DAI) [ 25 , 26 ]. The DAI scores were calculated as following grades: body weight loss (0–0%, 1–1%–5%, 2–5%–10%, 3–10%–20%, 4- > 20%), stool consistency (0-normal, 1- soft stools, 2-loose stools, 3- diarrhoea), rectal bleeding (0-normal, 1-a little bleeding of stool, 2- large area bleeding of stool, 3-gross bleeding). After one week, the colons of the mice were harvested, photographed, and their lengths measured. The DAI was calculated using the formula: DAI = (body weight loss + stool consistency + rectal bleeding)/3.

Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) was conducted to transfer gut microbiota from CSD donor mice to recipient mice. In brief, fresh fecal samples were collected from CSD mice, placed in a cryoprotectant of 10% glycerin and 90% PBS, and stored at − 80 °C until further use. Prior to FMT, recipient mice underwent a two-week pretreatment with an antibiotic cocktail (ABX) delivered via drinking water to deplete their native gut microbiota. The ABX regimen included ampicillin (0.5 g/L), neomycin sulfate (0.5 g/L), metronidazole (0.5 g/L), and vancomycin (0.25 g/L). For transplantation, fecal samples from CSD mice were resuspended in sterile PBS at a concentration of 100 mg/mL and thoroughly vortexed to achieve complete homogenization. The suspension was then centrifuged at 500 × g for 3 min to pellet insoluble debris. The clarified supernatant was collected and administered to ABX-pretreated recipient mice (F-CSD group) by oral gavage at a volume of 100 μL per mouse. The control group mice (F-Ctrl group) received microbiota from the Ctrl group mice. This procedure was repeated once daily over a period of 21 consecutive days to ensure sustained microbiota engraftment.

The mice were randomly divided into three groups: the Ctrl group, the CSD group, and the CSD + Taurine group (CSD + T), with 6 mice in each group. The CSD + T group underwent chronic sleep deprivation and was administered 200 mg/kg of taurine (HY-B0351, MedChemExpress, Beijing Anxinkang Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, China) via oral gavage daily at ZT4 time point for 21 days, with body weight measured every two days. Taurine was dissolved in pure water to form a clear and transparent solution. Meanwhile, the CSD group was given an equivalent volume of pure water daily, and the Ctrl group was maintained under normal conditions. After 21 days, the mice were uniformly euthanized at the ZT12 time point to collect samples for subsequent molecular biological assays.

The treatment protocol for CSD mice using SR8278 (KM7220, Kekule Biomedical Co., Ltd., Guangzhou, China), and taurine: Randomly divide the mice into 4 groups, namely Control, CSD, CSD + SR8278, CSD + SR8278 + Taurine (CSD + SR8278 + T). Each group consists of 6 mice. The CSD group only undergoes chronic sleep deprivation. The CSD + SR8278 group is given intraperitoneal injection of SR8278 at 25 mg/kg/day on top of chronic sleep deprivation. SR8278 is dissolved in 5% DMSO and 95% (20% SBE-β-CD (KM15751, Kekule Biomedical Co., Ltd., Guangzhou, China) in saline). The CSD + SR8278 + T group is given SR8278 and taurine at 200 mg/kg/day (gavage). The administration time is uniformly set at ZT4. After 21 days, the mice are sacrificed at the ZT12 time point and samples are collected uniformly.

Complete gastrointestinal transit time (GITT) was measured by administering 6% natural carmine red ( C82561 , ACMEC, Shanghai, China) dissolved in 0.5% methylcellulose (9085–26-1, ACMEC, Shanghai, China) by gavage (100 μL) according to Michael D Gershon [ 27 ]. Ctrl and CSD mice were starved 6 h prior togavage. Time of gavage was considered T0. In case of presence, fecal pellets were taken out of the cage every 10 min and checked for red color. GITT was registered as the time between T0 and the time of presence of carmine red in the fecal pellets.

At the end of all animal experiments, euthanasia was performed on the mice by cervical dislocation at ZT12. Colon tissues were carefully excised and gently rinsed with ice-cold PBS to remove luminal contents. A segment of approximately 1 cm of the distal colon (near the anal region) was collected and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (G1101-500 mL, Servicebio, Wuhan, China) for 24 h. Following fixation, the tissues were embedded in paraffin blocks. Transverse sections of the colon were prepared using a microtome (Thermo Scientific Microm HM 325, Shanghai, China), yielding 5-μm-thick sections. The paraffin-embedded sections were deparaffinized using an eco-friendly dewaxing solution and subsequently rehydrated through a graded series of alcohol solutions. For H&E staining (G1005-100 mL, Servicebio, Wuhan, China), sections were immersed in hematoxylin for 15 min, followed by differentiation in acid alcohol for 10 s. The sections were then counterstained with eosin for 5 min, dehydrated, and mounted with a coverslip. The prepared slides were scanned using a slide scanner for further analysis.

At the end of all animal experiments, mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation at ZT12, and the colons were collected. For immunohistochemical analysis, paraffin-embedded tissue sections were first deparaffinized using xylene and rehydrated through a graded series of ethanol solutions (100%, 95%, and 70%). Antigen retrieval was performed by incubating the sections in citrate buffer (pH 6.0) at 95 °C for 20 min, followed by cooling to room temperature. Endogenous peroxidase activity was quenched by treating the sections with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 10 min. Non-specific binding sites were blocked by incubating the sections with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA, GC305010-5 g, Servicebio, Wuhan, China) in Tris-buffered saline (TBS) for 1 h at room temperature. The sections were then incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer. After washing with TBS containing 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST), the sections were incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Immunoreactivity was visualized using 3,3'-diaminobenzidine (DAB, G1212-200 T, Servicebio, Wuhan, China) as the chromogen, and the sections were counterstained with hematoxylin to highlight nuclei. Finally, the sections were dehydrated, cleared in xylene, and mounted with a coverslip using a permanent mounting medium. Stained slides were imaged using a light microscope, and quantitative analysis was performed using imageJ analysis software. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining was performed using the PAS staining kit (G1008-20 mL, Servicebio, Wuhan, China).

Quantitative Immunohistochemical Methods: In this study, the quantitative analysis of IHC staining results was standardized using ImageJ software (version 1.8.0.112). All tissue sections were stained under identical experimental conditions, including primary antibody concentration, incubation time, and DAB chromogenic intensity. Briefly, the images were uniformly adjusted for contrast using the Brightness/Contrast function of ImageJ, maintaining consistent parameters. The Color Deconvolution plugin was utilized to separate dual-channel signals, retaining only the DAB channel for subsequent analysis to exclude interference from nuclear staining. Threshold processing was applied to the DAB channel image, employing the Otsu algorithm to automatically determine the threshold range, followed by manual fine-tuning to ensure the complete selection of positive regions (brown). Image optimization was performed using the Process > Binary function to generate a binarized image, with positive regions in white and the background in black. In the Set Measurements, the Integrated Density value was calculated to reflect the total amount of positive signal. Each field of view was measured three times, and the average value was taken as the representative value for the sample.

At the end of all animal experiments, mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation at ZT12. Colon tissues were collected and homogenized in RIPA lysis buffer (P0013C, Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (1 × , P1008, Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) using a tissue homogenizer (SRT-24, Sailt Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, China) at 60 Hz for 90 s. The homogenate was centrifuged at 13,000 × g for 15 min, and the supernatant was collected. Protein concentrations were determined using the BCA protein assay kit (PC0020, Solarbio, Beijing, China) and adjusted to ensure equal loading. For Western blot analysis, proteins were separated on a 10% SDS–polyacrylamide gel and subsequently transferred onto a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF, Millipore, Beijing, China) membrane. The membrane was blocked with 5% BSA for 1 h at room temperature, followed by incubation with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. The next day, the membrane was incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using an Omni-ECL™ Ultra-Sensitive Chemiluminescence Detection Kit (SQ201L, Epizyme, Shanghai, China) detection reagent on an E-Blot (Pro, EBLOT, Shanghai, China) imaging system. The intensity of target protein bands was quantified using ImageJ software. Detailed information of the antibodies utilized in the study is as follows in Table 1 .

Antibody information

Colon tissues were homogenized in TRIzol (ET111-01-V2, TransGen, Beijing, China) reagent using a tissue homogenizer at 60 Hz for 90 s. The homogenate was centrifuged at 13,000 × g for 15 min, and the supernatant was collected. Chloroform (200 μL) was added to the supernatant, followed by centrifugation at 13,000 × g for 15 min. The aqueous phase was transferred to a new tube, and an equal volume of isopropanol was added to precipitate the RNA. After centrifugation at 13,000 × g for 10 min, the RNA pellet was washed with 75% ethanol and dissolved in 100 μL of RNase-free water. RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using a reverse transcription kit (AU341-02-V2 TransGen, Beijing, China). Gene expression levels were analyzed using the CFX96 Real-Time PCR System (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). The primer sequences used were as follows in Table 2 .

Primers used in qPCR

Collect mouse feces using sterile 1.5 mL tubes, two pellets per mouse. Genomic DNA was extracted from the samples using the CTAB/SDS method. Specific regions of the 16S rRNA gene were amplified by PCR, and the PCR products were purified using the Qiagen Gel Extraction Kit (Qiagen, Germany). Sequencing libraries were constructed using the TruSeq® DNA PCR-Free Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina, USA). The quality of the libraries was assessed on a Qubit® 2.0 Fluorometer (Thermo Scientific, USA), and sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq platform to generate 250 bp paired-end reads.

Mouse fecal samples were collected and prepared for non-targeted metabolomics analysis. Briefly, feces were thawed on ice, and proteins were precipitated by mixing with ice-cold methanol (LC/MS grade, CAS:64–18-6) or acetonitrile (LC/MS grade, CAS:75–05-8, typically at a 1:3 or 1:4 ratio, feces:solvent). The mixture was vortexed thoroughly, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 × g for 15 min at 4 °C to remove proteins. The supernatant was collected and dried under a gentle stream of nitrogen. The dried metabolites were reconstituted in a suitable solvent (water:acetonitrile 1:1) for subsequent analysis.

Non-targeted metabolomics profiling was performed by a Novo Source Bio Company using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS). Chromatographic separation was achieved on a C18 column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.7 μm) with a gradient elution of mobile phases consisting of water (containing 0.1% formic acid) and acetonitrile. Mass spectrometry analysis was conducted in both positive and negative ionization modes using a high-resolution mass spectrometer (Q-TOF). Raw data were processed using proprietary software (Progenesis) for peak detection, alignment, and annotation against metabolomics databases (HMDB, Metlin, or KEGG).

Data were presented as mean ± SD of the results from at least 3 independent experiments. Data were analyzed by ONE-WAY ANOVA or TWO-WAY ANOVA analysis of variance or Student’s t test as appropriate, with significance set as p < 0.05 (*), p < 0.01 (**), p < 0.001 (***), p < 0.0001 (****).
sections.results:
To establish a chronic sleep deprivation (CSD) model, mice were placed in a motorized apparatus (mechanical intervention) that prevented sleep from 18:00 to 14:00 the following day (Fig. 1 A). By day 3, compared to the Ctrl group, the CSD mice exhibited a significant body weight loss of approximately 5.62%. Although body weight gradually recovered after CSD, it remained lower than that of control mice even 15 days post-deprivation (Fig. 1 B, C ). To assess the impact of CSD on intestinal health, the colon length was measured and found to be significantly shorter in CSD mice compared to controls (Fig. 1 D, E ). Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining revealed mild inflammatory cell infiltration between the submucosa and muscularis layers in CSD mice, in contrast to the control group, which showed no such changes (Fig. 1 F). These findings suggest that CSD may initiate early inflammatory responses and structural alterations in the colon.

F H&E staining of distal colon tissues. G Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) staining for goblet cells in colon tissue. H Quantification of goblet cell numbers shown in ( G ), performed using ImageJ software. I , K , M Immunohistochemical staining of colon tissue, where brown represents Muc2 ( I ), Occludin ( K ), and Claudin-1 ( M ), respectively, and blue represents the nuclei. J , L , N The expression levels of Muc2, Occludin, and Claudin-1 in ( I , K , M ) were quantitatively analyzed using ImageJ. O , P qPCR was employed to detect the mRNA expression of Claudin-1 and Occludin in colonic tissues, with β-actin as the internal reference. Q Western blot was used to detect the protein expression levels of Claudin-1 and Occludin in colonic tissues. R , S The gray values of Claudin-1 and Occludin in ( Q ) were quantified using ImageJ and compared with that of β-actin. (n = 4 to 6). Data are expressed as means ± SD. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001

Given the critical role of the intestinal barrier in preventing pathogen invasion and maintaining immune homeostasis, we next evaluated mucosal barrier integrity. PAS staining further demonstrated a marked decrease in goblet cell numbers in the CSD group, indicating impaired mucus secretion and barrier function (Fig. 1 G, H ). Immunohistochemical staining for Mucin 2 (Muc2), a key mucosal glycoprotein, revealed significantly reduced expression in CSD mice (F i g. 1 I, J ). Consistent with these findings, both immunohistochemistry and molecular analyses showed that the expression of tight junction proteins Occludin and Claudin-1 was significantly downregulated in CSD mice (Fig. 1 K–N). Western blot and qPCR confirmed significant reductions in both protein and mRNA levels of Occludin and Claudin-1 following CSD (Fig. 1 O–S). Together, these data indicate that CSD compromises intestinal barrier integrity by disrupting mucus production and downregulating tight junction proteins.

Disruption of the intestinal barrier increases susceptibility to mucosal inflammation and is a key contributor to the pathogenesis of colitis. To examine the impact of CSD on colitis progression, mice were administered 2.5% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) in drinking water for 7 days to induce colitis, with concurrent CSD treatment. Control mice were maintained under standard conditions without DSS or CSD exposure (Fig. 2 A). DSS treatment alone led to a significant reduction in colon length compared to controls, while CSD with DSS group exhibited an even more pronounced shortening of the colon (Fig. 2 B, C ). Body weight loss was most severe in the CSD with DSS group, followed by the DSS group, with control animals showing the least reduction (Fig. 2 D). Disease Activity Index (DAI) scores followed a similar trend, with significantly higher values observed in the CSD with DSS group compared to the DSS group and control group (Fig. 2 E), indicating that CSD exacerbates the clinical severity of colitis. Histological analysis using H&E staining revealed enhanced inflammatory cell infiltration in the colonic tissue of the CSD with DSS group relative to DSS alone (Fig. 2 F). Immunohistochemical staining showed further reductions in Muc2 and Occludin expression in the CSD with DSS group compared to DSS-only mice (Fig. 2 G–J), suggesting additional compromise of the mucosal barrier. These observations were validated by qPCR and Western blot analyses, which demonstrated the greatest reductions in both mRNA and protein levels of Occludin and Claudin-1 in the CSD with DSS group (Fig. 2 K–N). At the molecular level, the expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine Il-10 was lowest in the CSD with DSS group, whereas pro-inflammatory markers Il-6 and Il-1β were significantly elevated compared to the DSS group (Fig. 2 O–Q). Together, these findings suggest that CSD exacerbates DSS-induced colitis, potentially by impairing barrier integrity and amplifying intestinal inflammation.

The gut microbiota, often referred to as the “second genome”, plays a critical role in maintaining intestinal homeostasis, and its dysregulation is a major contributor to epithelial barrier disruption and mucosal inflammation. To explore whether CSD affects gut microbial composition, we collected fresh fecal samples from control and CSD-treated mice for 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Principal component analysis (PCA) of the sequencing data revealed a clear separation between the two groups, with PC1 and PC2 accounting for 19.27% and 18.26% of the total variance, respectively (Fig. 3 A). This separation indicates that CSD induces substantial shifts in gut microbial communities. Taxonomic profiling showed that, at the class and family levels, CSD was associated with an increased relative abundance of Bacteroidia and Muribaculaceae , and a decreased abundance of Clostridia and Lachnospiraceae (Fig. 3 B, C ). Microbial alpha diversity was significantly reduced in the CSD group, as evidenced by lower Chao1 diversity and observed feature richness compared to controls (Fig. 3 D, E ), suggesting an overall loss of microbial complexity. Venn diagram analysis further demonstrated that the CSD group harbored 1037 unique operational taxonomic units (OTUs), compared to 1366 in the control group, with 670 OTUs shared between the two groups (Fig. 3 F). Most of these shared OTUs were affiliated with the phylum Firmicutes , and the genera Ligilactobacillus and Dubosiella, and the family Lachnospiraceae were significantly more abundant in the control group (Fig. 3 G). Differential abundance analysis identified several key taxa altered by sleep deprivation. Notably, the beneficial Akkermansiaceae family was markedly reduced in the CSD group, while potentially pathogenic or inflammation-associated taxa, including Ralstonia , Acetivibrio ethanolgignens , Anaerostipes , Allobaculum , and Burkholderiaceae -were significantly increased (Fig. 3 H–M). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that CSD disrupts gut microbiota composition, characterized by a decrease in beneficial commensals and an enrichment of pathogenic bacteria. This dysbiosis may contribute to intestinal barrier impairment and inflammation associated with sleep deprivation.

Chronic sleep deprivation alters gut microbiota composition and reduces microbial diversity. To determine whether gut microbiota contributes to CSD-induced intestinal barrier disruption, we performed fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) by transferring microbiota from CSD mice into antibiotic-pretreated recipient mice. To promote engraftment and eliminate interference from endogenous microbes, recipient mice were administered a broad-spectrum antibiotic cocktail (ABX) for two weeks prior to transplantation (Fig. 4 A). Although ABX can eliminate the vast majority of intestinal microorganisms, it still cannot achieve a completely sterile state (SI-Fig. 1 A-C). Consequently, it was necessary to verify the similarity in intestinal microbiota diversity between the F-CSD and CSD groups. Analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data revealed no significant differences between the F-CSD and CSD groups in terms of principal component distribution, α-diversity, or β-diversity (SI-Fig. 1 D-G). These findings confirm that the FMT approach successfully enabled the colonization of microbiota derived from CSD mice in the recipient mice.

Transplantation from sleep-deprived mice induces disruption of intestinal barrier integrity in antibiotic-treated recipients. While body weight did not differ significantly between F-CSD and F-Ctrl mice (Fig. 4 B), F-CSD mice exhibited significantly shorter colon length, suggesting compromised intestinal integrity (Fig. 4 C, D ). Histological analysis revealed marked inflammatory cell infiltration and a substantial decrease in goblet cell numbers in F-CSD colons (Fig. 4 E–G), indicating mucosal damage. To further assess barrier function, we evaluated the expression of the mucus layer protein Muc2 and the tight junction proteins Claudin-1 and Occludin. Immunohistochemical staining revealed a significant reduction of Muc2 in F-CSD mice (Fig. 4 H, I ), consistent with impaired mucosal protection. Furthermore, both immunohistochemistry and Western blot analysis, supported by qPCR, showed significantly decreased expression of Claudin-1 and Occludin at the mRNA and protein levels in F-CSD mice (Fig. 4 J–R). These findings collectively demonstrate that gut microbiota derived from sleep-deprived mice is sufficient to disrupt intestinal barrier function, highlighting its essential role in mediating the detrimental effects of CSD on gut homeostasis.

To elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying CSD-induced intestinal barrier dysfunction, we performed RNA sequencing on intestinal epithelial tissues from control and CSD mice. PCA revealed a clear separation between the two groups along PC1 and PC2, indicating substantial transcriptomic alterations following CSD (Fig. 5 A). Differential expression analysis identified 1,188 upregulated and 308 downregulated genes in the CSD group compared to control (Fig. 5 B). KEGG pathway enrichment analysis revealed that differentially expressed genes were significantly enriched in the circadian rhythm pathway (Fig. 5 C), suggesting that CSD perturbs the expression of intestinal clock genes.

Chronic sleep deprivation disrupts circadian rhythms in intestinal epithelial tissues. A PCA of intestinal epithelium tissue based on RNA-seq analysis. B The volcano plot displays the differentially expressed genes in CSD compared to control. C KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes. D Schematic diagram of intestinal epithelial tissue collected at 6 different time points (ZT: Zeitgeber time, hours after the start of the light period). E , F qPCR analysis of Bmal1 and Nr1d1 mRNA expression in the intestinal epithelium tissues of the control and CSD at different time points. G Western blot analysis of Bmal1, and Nr1d1 protein expression in the intestinal epithelium tissues of the control and CSD at different time points. H , I Quantification of Nr1d1 and Bmal1 in ( G ) was performed using ImageJ (n = 4 to 6). Data are expressed as means ± SD. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, **** p < 0.0001

To investigate this further, we analyzed the temporal expression patterns of key circadian regulators Nr1d1 and Bmal1 , both previously implicated in colonic inflammation [ 21 , 28 ]. Intestinal epithelial tissues were collected at six time points (ZT0, ZT4, ZT8, ZT12, ZT16, ZT20) over a 24-h period. We observed that CSD significantly downregulated Nr1d1 expression, whereas Bmal1 expression was markedly elevated (Fig. 5 D–F). This is consistent with the known regulatory relationship in which Nr1d1 directly represses Bmal1 transcription. At the protein level, Western blot analysis mirrored the mRNA results, showing elevated Bmal1 and reduced Nr1d1 expression in CSD mice (F i g. 5 G–I). These findings suggest that CSD disrupts the intestinal epithelial circadian clock via downregulation of Nr1d1 and subsequent derepression of Bmal1. Interestingly, the mRNA expression levels of the other three clock gene Clock , Per1 , and Cry1 did not exhibit significant changes (SI-Fig. 2 A-C). This could be attributed to the fact that chronic sleep deprivation specifically impacts the Nr1d1-Bmal1 pathway, with Nr1d1 or Bmal1 presumably serving as its direct target gene, whereas its influence on other circadian clock genes remains relatively minimal. Given the role of gut microbiota in modulating host circadian gene expression, our results imply that microbiota-mediated suppression of Nr1d1 may contribute to CSD-induced barrier dysfunction and inflammatory responses in the gut.

To further elucidate the mechanisms by which gut microbiota contributes to sleep deprivation-induced intestinal inflammation, we performed untargeted metabolomic profiling of fecal samples collected immediately after completion of the CSD model. PCA revealed a clear separation between the control and CSD groups, indicating significant differences in overall metabolic profiles (Fig. 6 A). Differential metabolite analysis showed that, compared to the control group, 627 metabolites were upregulated, 207 were downregulated, and 975 remained unchanged in the CSD group (Fig. 6 B). Functional annotation revealed that these differential metabolites were mainly involved in Cellular Processes, Genetic Information Processing, Metabolism, Organismal Systems, and Environmental Information Processing, with metabolic pathways accounting for the largest proportion (Fig. 6 C).

Disruption of taurine metabolism links gut microbial dysbiosis to intestinal injury under sleep deprivation. A PCA was performed on the untargeted microbial metabolites of control and CSD mice. B The volcano plot displays differential metabolites. C Functional enrichment analysis of differential metabolites. D Conduct KEGG enrichment pathway analysis on metabolites associated with metabolic functions. E The CSD group, compared to the control group, characterized the top 10 differential metabolites, with red indicating upregulation and blue indicating downregulation. F , G The levels of Taurocholic acid and Taurolithocholic acid associated with taurine-conjugated metabolites in different groups. H , I The relative expression of microbiota Lactobacillus and Bilophila wadsworthia , which are closely associated with taurine, in the CSD and control groups, as derived from the 16S rRNA sequencing results in Fig. 3

To identify key metabolic pathways affected by sleep deprivation, we performed KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the metabolism-related differential metabolites. Notably, taurine and hypotaurine metabolism emerged as significantly altered pathways (Fig. 6 D). Among the top 10 differential metabolites, taurine was markedly reduced in the CSD group compared to controls (Fig. 6 E). Conjugated taurine derivatives, such as taurocholic acid and taurolithocholic acid, were also significantly decreased (Fig. 6 F, G ). Furthermore, in the CSD group, the microbiota genera Lactobacillus and Bilophila wadsworthia , which are closely associated with taurine levels, were significantly reduced (Fig. 6 H, I ) [ 29 , 30 ]. These findings suggest that sleep deprivation leads to a depletion of taurine and its metabolites, implicating impaired microbial taurine metabolism as a potential contributor to intestinal barrier dysfunction and inflammation.

To investigate the therapeutic potential of taurine in mitigating sleep deprivation-induced intestinal barrier damage, we administered taurine via oral gavage to mice subjected to CSD (CSD + T), while the CSD group received an equal volume of water (Fig. 7 A). After three weeks of treatment, mice in the CSD group exhibited significant weight loss, whereas taurine supplementation significantly ameliorated weight loss (Fig. 7 B). Moreover, taurine-treated mice displayed significantly longer colon lengths compared to the CSD group (Fig. 7 C, D ), suggesting a protective effect on intestinal integrity. H&E staining revealed that the inflammatory cell infiltration observed in the colonic mucosa of CSD mice was markedly reduced following taurine treatment, with tissue morphology resembling that of control mice (Fig. 7 E). To assess whether taurine could repair intestinal barrier dysfunction, we examined the expression of tight junction proteins. Both mRNA and protein levels of Claudin-1 and Occludin, which were downregulated by sleep deprivation, were significantly restored following taurine treatment (Fig. 7 F–J), indicating enhanced barrier integrity.

Taurine supplementation ameliorates sleep deprivation-induced intestinal injury. A Schematic diagram of sleep deprivation and taurine (T) administration. B The body weights of mice in each group were recorded after the completion of taurine treatment. C Representative image of mouse colon. D Statistical analysis of the colon length in ( C ). E Representative images of HE staining in mouse colon. F , G qPCR was employed to detect the mRNA expression of Claudin-1 and Occludin in the intestinal epithelium tissues, with β-actin as the internal reference. ( H ) The expression levels of Claudin-1 and Occludin proteins in the intestinal epithelium tissues were detected by Western blot. I , J The gray values of Claudin-1 and Occludin in ( H ) were quantified using ImageJ and compared with that of β-actin. K The expression levels of Nr1d1 and Bmal1 proteins in the intestinal epithelium tissues were detected by Western blot. L , M The gray values of Nr1d1 and Bmal1 in ( K ) were quantified using ImageJ and compared with that of β-actin (n = 4 to 6). Data are expressed as means ± SD. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001

Furthermore, taurine treatment reversed the dysregulation of intestinal circadian clock genes induced by CSD. Specifically, the downregulated expression of Nr1d1 and the upregulated expression of its downstream target Bmal1 were normalized to control levels after taurine administration (Fig. 7 K–M). Furthermore, we also investigated whether the upregulation of Nr1d1 expression by taurine is time-dependent. We detected the changes in Nr1d1 expression in the intestinal epithelial tissues of CSD mice treated with taurine at different time points. The Western blot results showed that in the taurine treatment group, Nr1d1 was significantly upregulated at all four time points (ZT0, ZT6, ZT12, ZT18) (SI-Fig. 3 A-C). Meanwhile, taurine can also inhibit the expression of Bmal1 at the ZT0 and ZT12 time points (SI-Fig. 3 B, D ). Furthermore, the qPCR results showed that taurine had no significant effect on Per1 and Cry1 (SI-Fig. 3 E, F ). It is indicated that the upregulation of Nr1d1 by taurine is not time-dependent. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that taurine ameliorates sleep deprivation-induced intestinal inflammation and barrier dysfunction, potentially by targeting the nuclear receptor NR1D1.

To further investigate the the potential role of Nr1d1 in treating the intestinal barrier dysfunction in mice with CSD, we subjected mice to CSD and administered the NR1D1 antagonist SR8278 with or without taurine (Fig. 8 A). Following three weeks of intervention, the CSD group exhibited significantly lower body weight compared to the control group. Mice treated with SR8278 alone showed no significant body weight difference from the CSD group, though a downward trend was observed. Notably, concurrent administration of SR8278 and taurine resulted in a significant weight gain, with body weights significantly higher than those in the SR8278 monotherapy group (Fig. 8 B). Histopathological analysis of mouse colons via H&E staining revealed that SR8278 monotherapy exacerbated colonic mucosal injury in CSD mice, characterized by disorganized tissue architecture. In contrast, combined treatment with SR8278 and taurine preserved colonic mucosal integrity, with well-organized tissue structure and intact cellular morphology (Fig. 8 C). These findings indicate that SR8278 exacerbates intestinal mucosal damage in CSD mice, while taurine can reverse the detrimental effects of SR8278 on the colon under CSD conditions. Western blot analysis demonstrated that SR8278 downregulated the expression of the intestinal barrier-related protein Occludin in CSD mice, whereas taurine restored Occludin expression suppressed by SR8278 (Fig. 8 D, E ). Immunohistochemical analysis of Claudin-1 and PAS staining for goblet cell labeling further confirmed that taurine reversed the SR8278-induced inhibition of Claudin-1 expression and reduction in goblet cell numbers (F i g. 8 F–I).

Taurine reverses NR1D1 antagonist-exacerbated intestinal barrier dysfunction in chronic sleep deprivation. A Schematic diagram of the treatment of CSD model mice with SR8278 and taurine (T). B Body weight of the mice. C Representative images of HE staining of the mouse colon. D Western blot analysis of the protein expression levels of Occludin and Nr1d1 in the intestinal epithelial tissue of mice, with β-actin as the internal control. E Quantification of the expression levels of Occludin in ( D ) using ImageJ, compared to β-actin. F Immunohistochemical detection of Claudin-1 (brown) expression in the colon tissue of mice, with nuclei stained blue. G Quantification of Claudin-1 in ( F ) using ImageJ. H PAS staining marks glycogen (pink) in the mouse colon, with nuclei appearing blue. I Goblet cells in ( H ) were quantified using ImageJ (n = 4 to 6)

Collectively, these results suggest that the NR1D1 antagonist SR8278 exacerbates intestinal barrier dysfunction in CSD mice, and taurine can reverse this effect. This implies that taurine may exert therapeutic effects on intestinal barrier dysfunction by targeting NR1D1.
sections.discussion:
Insufficient sleep imposes profound stress on the digestive system, markedly aggravating the burden of IBD [ 31 , 32 ]. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms, we established a chronic sleep deprivation mouse model and observed that intestinal barrier integrity was significantly impaired. Transcriptome analysis demonstrated that CSD significantly suppresses the expression of the Nr1d1 in intestinal epithelial cells, while concurrently upregulating the expression of Bmal1. Mechanistic investigations revealed that this impairment was driven by disruptions in microbial metabolites. Notably, sleep deprivation led to a marked reduction in microbiota-derived taurine, which in turn dysregulated the expression of the core circadian clock factor Nr1d1 in intestinal epithelial cells. This dysregulation suppressed the expression of critical barrier-associated proteins, including Claudin-1 and Occludin, thereby contributing to compromised barrier function and promoting colitis pathogenesis.

In this study, we observed a significant reduction in both the α-diversity and Chao1 index of the gut microbiota in mice subjected to chronic sleep deprivation, indicating that sleep deprivation leads to dysbiosis of the gut microbiota. Sleep deprivation may disrupt gut microbiota homeostasis through various pathways, including neuroendocrine disturbances, compromised immune defenses, alterations in the gut environment, and dysregulation of the gut-brain axis [ 33 ]. Furthermore, gastrointestinal transit time (GITT) and food intake are significant factors contributing to gut microbiota dysbiosis. Researchers have indicated that rapid gastrointestinal transit favors the proliferation of fast-growing bacteria, whereas slow transit promotes fermentation and the metabolic processes of slow-growing microorganisms [ 34 ]. In this study, we established a sleep deprivation model by inducing forced exercise in mice, necessitating consideration of the effects of this method on their eating, drinking, and gastrointestinal transit. Statistical analyses revealed that food and water intake in the CSD group were both significantly lower than those in the control group (SI-Fig. 4 A, B ). Conversely, the GITT time was longer in the CSD group compared to the control group (CSD: 105.3 min vs. Ctrl: 99.5 min) (SI-Fig. 4 C). These findings indicate that chronic sleep deprivation can lead to a reduction in food and water intake in mice, as well as an increase in GITT time. The findings indicate that our sleep deprivation model is inherently multifactorial. As a mechanical intervention–based paradigm, it not only induces sleep deficiency but also introduces additional non-specific stressors (e.g., those exemplified by the water avoidance stress model) beyond sleep loss [ 35 ]. These extraneous factors are likely to co-contribute to gut microbiota dysbiosis and barrier dysfunction. Accordingly, we refer to our paradigm throughout the manuscript as “mechanical intervention–based sleep deprivation”, a term that more accurately reflects the composite nature of this model.

Furthurmore, the circadian rhythm of the gut microbiota, often referred to as the "microbial oscillator," is a fundamental aspect of host metabolic and immune homeostasis [ 33 , 36 , 37 ]. This spatiotemporal distribution lays the groundwork for the rhythmic production of microbial metabolites. For instance, Lactobacillus , a core member of the Firmicutes phylum known for producing taurine, reaches peak abundance during the dark phase [ 38 , 39 ]. Although direct data on the rhythmicity of taurine are currently lacking, it is reasonable to hypothesize that the intestinal concentration of taurine may synchronize with the proliferation cycle of Lactobacillus , with vigorous synthesis expected during the dark phase (the active period for mice), followed by gradual accumulation during the light phase (the resting period) [ 39 , 40 ]. Notably, this study observed that the protein expression peaks of the nuclear receptor Nr1d1 occur at the mid-light phase (ZT12), a timing that potentially corresponds with the hypothesized taurine accumulation period (transition from dark to light phase) [ 40 ]. While direct detection of dynamic fluctuations in taurine has not been conducted, the logical framework aligns closely with the interaction pattern of "microbiota rhythm-metabolite -host clock" reported in existing literature. Future research should aim to verify the diurnal curve of taurine through 24-h dynamic monitoring to establish a theoretical foundation for temporal intervention.

NR1D1, a pivotal member of the nuclear receptor family involved in the circadian clock, plays a critical role in the regulation of inflammation. Its mechanism of action includes the direct inhibition of pro-inflammatory factor expression, modulation of metabolic pathways, and synergistic interactions with other circadian clock genes [ 21 , 41 , 42 ]. In the LPS-induced bovine endometrial epithelial cell (BEND) model, elevated expression of NR1D1 significantly suppresses the expression of pro-inflammatory factors such as IL-6, IL-8, and IL-1β, whereas the knockdown of NR1D1 exacerbates the inflammatory response [ 43 ]. This anti-inflammatory property also be relevant in IBD, particularly in ulcerative colitis (UC) patients who frequently experience persistent inflammation of the intestinal mucosa [ 44 ]. NR1D1 alleviate intestinal inflammation by inhibiting pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB/NLRP3, thereby reducing the release of TNF-α and IL-6 [ 21 ]. Furthermore, NR1D1 has been shown to regulate bile acid metabolism and the synthesis of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) [ 45 , 46 ]. The deficiency of SCFAs, such as butyrate, is closely associated with intestinal barrier damage and microbiota dysbiosis [ 47 ]. Collectively, these studies underscore the potential of targeting NR1D1 as a therapeutic strategy for the treatment of colitis. Our research demonstrates that sleep deprivation markedly suppresses Nr1d1 expression, thereby disrupting intestinal homeostasis.

Non-targeted metabolomics identified taurine as one of the most significantly downregulated microbiota-derived metabolites in CSD mice [ 48 , 49 ]. Exogenous taurine supplementation restored Nr1d1 expression, enhanced tight junction protein synthesis, and suppressed pro-inflammatory factor release, thereby reversing CSD-induced intestinal damage. This effect likely operates through several complementary pathways. First, taurine may directly activate Nr1d1, restoring its circadian regulatory function. The direct interaction mechanism between taurine and Nr1d1 remains unclear and necessitates validation through molecular docking or in vitro experiments. Secondly, previous studies have established that NF-κB transcriptionally represses Nr1d1 by binding to its promoter region [ 50 ]. Our findings further demonstrate that taurine suppresses NF-κB activation, thereby potentially restoring Nr1d1 expression (SI-Fig. 5 A, B ), consistent with the observations reported by Yuan et al. 51 . Third, the observed reductions in food intake and prolonged GITT can directly alter microbial composition and metabolite production, independent of the taurine pathway. Taken together, these results indicate that the “microbiota–taurine–Nr1d1 axis” constitutes an important mechanism underlying the effects of sleep deprivation on gut homeostasis, but it is unlikely to be the only pathway involved.

This study elucidates critical mechanisms of sleep deprivation–induced intestinal injury, yet several issues remain unresolved. First, the CSD model with 20-h continuous deprivation may not fully reflect clinical sleep fragmentation, highlighting the need for models that better mimic real-world conditions. Second, we did not evaluate circadian oscillations of the gut microbiota, which may substantially contribute to sleep deprivatio–related intestinal injury and warrant further investigation.
sections.conclusion: In summary, our findings elucidate the molecular mechanisms through which chronic sleep deprivation induces intestinal barrier damage and exacerbates the burden of colitis. We revealed a reduction in the key microbial metabolite taurine, which disrupts the normal expression of Nr1d1. This dysregulation ultimately leads to a decrease in the production of barrier proteins, resulting in early inflammation and worsening the burden of colitis. Additionally, we propose that Nr1d1 in intestinal epithelial cells may serve as a promising therapeutic target. Furthermore, we underscore the potential research value of taurine in treating digestive system diseases associated with sleep deprivation, thereby offering therapeutic strategies for future clinical interventions in such conditions.
